previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson was admitted for acute on chronic systolic heart failure exacerbation, presenting with worsening dyspnea, weight gain, and bilateral edema. His condition was complicated by a urinary tract infection with coagulase-negative staphylococcus, treated with IV ceftriaxone, and supertherapeutic INR and digoxin levels, both managed by temporary discontinuation and careful restart. He received IV furosemide and a diuretic drip, which was paused due to rising creatinine, then resumed as oral torsemide. Dobutamine was briefly used for perfusion support. His heart failure improved with diuresis, and he was transitioned to oral medications including losartan, with uptitration of hydralazine and isosorbide. He was discharged to extended care with stable vital signs, improved symptoms, and a weight of 133.6 kg.

ACTIVE ISSUES
=============
# Chest pain: The patient presented with intermittent 
non-exertional, non-radiating, sharp pain felt directly at site 
of his AICD. The first pain episode occurred while he was 
cooking breakfast and resolved after several minutes. Similar 
episodes recurred throughout the morning, which led the patient 
to call his nurse who advised him to go to the emergency room. 
The patient's chest pain recurred several times in the ED, but 
resolved without treatment. His ICD never fired. No EKG changes. 
Troponins 0.03 (his baseline), then decreased to 0.02 on the 
evening of admission, lowering suspicion of NSTEMI. Throughout 
hospitalization, he denied shortness of breath. His lungs 
remained clear and his lower extremities had minimal edema on 
exam, which decreased likelihood of acute heart failure. No 
pleuritic chest pain. No palpitations, lightheadedness, or 
syncope and no EKG changes or altered rhythm on telemetry. His 
chest pain did not recur on the floor. The patient received his 
home medications during admission and was discharged with no 
medication changes. Pain episodes were thought to be MSK in 
origin given the intermittent quality and subcutaneous location 
at the site of ICD.
